headline: 258 House seats. No party has won that many since 1992.
summary: Chuck Hubbard beat Virginia Foxx by 330 votes in North Carolina on Sunday, after a recount, and that seat took Democrats to 258. The party has gained 44 seats, four more than in 2018. Republicans hold 173, with four races still open. Hakeem Jeffries is in line to be Speaker on January 3. Trump still holds the veto on every bill.
cover_answer: No. Trump still has the veto. Investigations, yes.
table_question: If you won by a lot, would you still listen to the losing side?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The grown-ups who make the country's rules work in one big room with 435 chairs. The last election gave one team, the Democrats, 258 of those chairs, the most for one team since 1992, long before you were born. Picture a tug of war with far more people on one end of the rope. Nothing changes at our house.
5-7.why: Chairs and a rope make 258 something they can see. The count matters less than hearing that their day is the same.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them a room of chairs and a lopsided rope instead of a percentage. They read your face before your words, and a calm 'nothing changes at our house' is the message. Expect 'who's the boss now?' Nobody new. The president is still the president.

8-12.script: The House has 435 seats, and a bill needs 218 votes. Democrats won 258, so think of each vote as a race to 218: dozens of their runners can drop out and the rest still cross the line. Every bill still ends at Trump's desk, and he can veto it.
8-12.why: A race to 218 is a rule they can run themselves. The veto at the end is the fairness question they will ask about.
8-12.why_long: At nine they are working out chains of cause and effect, and this one is clean: 435 seats, 218 to pass, 258 in hand, so a few dropouts change nothing. Piaget's concrete stage reasons best with numbers it can line up. Expect 'then why can't they just do it?' The rule has one more step, and the president owns it: sign or veto.

13-17.script: What is a mandate worth with a veto at the other end? Democrats won 258 House seats and 56 in the Senate, so bills pass and subpoenas go out, but Trump signs or vetoes every law. Rep. Tom Suozzi wants 75% of their time on prices, 25% on investigations. Second: is that the right split?
13-17.why: Mandate and veto are both true. Suozzi's 75/25 split gives them a number to argue with instead of a slogan.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold a record majority and an unchanged veto in one thought, and Kuhn's point is that arguing from both is a skill that improves with practice. Suozzi's 75/25 split is a concrete claim to push on. Expect 'so what did the election change?' Who writes the bills and who gets subpoenaed. Not who signs them.

5-7.a: Nobody new. One team has more chairs, and the president is still the president.

8-12.q: Why is 258 such a big deal?
8-12.a: 218 votes pass a bill. With 258, dozens can vote no and it passes.

8-12.q: What about the four races not finished?
8-12.a: Two go to runoffs in December. Two are still being counted.

13-17.a: Through Congress, yes. Into law, no. Trump can veto any bill.
Jeffries hasn't ruled out a third try. Nobody has filed one.
